option_c: the ""balanced take-off distance"" equals 115% of the ""all engine take-off distance"".
option_d: the end of the runway will be cleared by 35 feet following an engine failure at V1.
explanation: If the aircraft's takeoff mass is limited by the Take-Off Distance Available (TODA), it means that the takeoff is field-length limited, and the actual takeoff mass is equal to the field-length-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: VR cannot be lower than:
option_a: V1 and 105% of VMCA.
option_c: 1.2 Vs for twin and three engine jet aeroplane.
option_d: 1.15 Vs for turbo-prop with three or more engines.
explanation: To ensure safety, the rotation speed VR cannot be less than the takeoff decision speed V1, and must be at least 105% of the air minimum control speed (VMCA).

question_text: V2 has to be equal to or higher than
option_a: 1.1 VMCA.
option_c: 1.1 VSO.
explanation: The takeoff safety speed V2 must be at least 1.1 * VMCA to provide an adequate speed margin above the minimum control speed in the air in case of engine failure.

question_text: V1 has to be
option_a: equal to or higher than VMCG.
option_b: equal to or higher than VMCA.
option_c: higher than than VR.
option_d: equal to or higher than V2.
explanation: V1 must be at least equal to VMCG to ensure that if an engine failure occurs at V1 and the pilot decides to reject the takeoff, they will have sufficient aerodynamic control (rudder) to keep the aircraft on the runway.

question_text: The speed VR
option_a: is the speed at which rotation to the lift-off angle of attack is initiated.
option_c: must be higher than VLOF.
option_d: must be equal to or lower than V1.
explanation: VR is the rotation speed, which is the airspeed at which the pilot begins to pull back on the yoke to rotate the aircraft to its takeoff attitude.

question_text: The speed V2 is
option_a: the take-off safety speed.
option_b: that speed at which the PIC should decide to continue or not the take-off in the case of an engine failure.
option_c: the lowest airspeed required to retract flaps without stall problems.
option_d: the lowest safety airspeed at which the aeroplane is under control with aerodynamic surfaces in the case of an engine failure.
explanation: V2 is the takeoff safety speed, which must be maintained during the initial climbout segment up to the acceleration altitude following an engine failure.

question_text: Which take-off speed is affected by the presence or absence of stopway and/or clearway ?
option_a: V1
option_c: VMCG
option_d: VMCA
explanation: The presence of a stopway or clearway changes the balance between the ASDA and TODA, which directly shifts the range of allowable V1 speeds (allowing a higher or lower V1 depending on which parameter is modified).

question_text: The speed V2 is defined for jet aeroplane as
option_a: take-off climb speed or speed at 35 ft.
option_c: take-off decision speed.
option_d: critical engine failure speed.
explanation: For jet aircraft, V2 is the takeoff safety speed or target climb speed that must be attained by the time the aircraft reaches a height of 35 feet above the runway during an engine-out takeoff.

question_text: The take-off mass could be limited by
option_a: the take-off distance available (TODA), the maximum brake energy and the climb gradient with one engine inoperative.
option_c: the climb gradient with one engine inoperative only.
option_d: the take-off distance available (TODA) only.
explanation: The maximum takeoff mass can be limited by several factors: the field length available (TODA/ASDA), the structural limits, the maximum energy the brakes can absorb during a reject (brake energy limit), or the maximum rotational speed of the tyres (tyre speed limit).

question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to VMCA (air minimum control speed)?
option_a: Straight flight can not be maintained below VMCA, when the critical engine has failed.
option_b: The aeroplane is uncontrollable below VMCA
option_c: The aeroplane will not gather the minimum required climb gradient
option_d: VMCA only applies to four-engine aeroplanes
explanation: VMCA is the minimum speed at which it is possible to maintain straight flight with a maximum of 5° of bank when the critical engine is inoperative and the other engine is at maximum takeoff power.

question_text: Which of the following will decrease V1?
option_a: Inoperative anti-skid.
option_c: Inoperative flight management system.
option_d: Increased outside air temperature.
explanation: If the anti-skid system is inoperative, the braking efficiency during a rejected takeoff is severely degraded, which increases the stopping distance. To compensate and ensure the aircraft can stop within the ASDA, the decision speed V1 must be decreased.

question_text: In case of an engine failure recognized below V1
option_a: the take-off must be rejected.
option_b: the take-off may be continued if a clearway is available.
option_c: the take-off should only be rejected if a stopway is available.
option_d: the take-off is to be continued unless V1 is less than the balanced V1.
explanation: If an engine failure occurs below V1, the aircraft is at a speed where there is sufficient runway remaining to safely bring the aircraft to a stop, so the takeoff must be rejected.

question_text: In case of an engine failure which is recognized at or above V1
option_a: the take-off must be continued.
option_b: the take-off must be rejected if the speed is still below VLOF.
option_c: a height of 50 ft must be reached within the take-off distance.
option_d: the take-off should be rejected if the speed is still below VR.
explanation: At or above V1, the aircraft has passed the point where it can safely stop on the remaining runway. Therefore, the takeoff must be continued, climbing out on the remaining engine(s).

question_text: The take-off distance available is
option_a: the length of the take-off run available plus the length of the clearway available.
option_c: the runway length plus half of the clearway.
option_d: the total runway length, without clearway even if this one exists.
explanation: TODA is defined as the Take-Off Run Available (TORA) plus the length of any clearway (an obstacle-free area beyond the runway under airport control).

question_text: The take-off safety speed V2min for turbo-propeller powered aeroplanes with more than three engines may not be less than:
option_c: 1.2 Vs
explanation: Under certification regulations, the minimum takeoff safety speed V2 min for turboprop aircraft with four or more engines is defined as 1.15 * VS (where VS is the stall speed in takeoff configuration).

question_text: The take-off safety speed V2 for two-engined or three-engined turbo propeller powered aeroplanes may not be less than:
option_a: 1.2 Vs
explanation: Under certification regulations, the minimum takeoff safety speed V2 min for two- or three-engine turboprop aircraft is defined as 1.2 * VS to ensure an adequate margin above the stall speed.

question_text: Which statement regarding V1 is correct ?
option_a: VR may not be lower than V1
option_b: V1 may not be higher than Vmcg
option_c: When determining V1, reverse thrust may only be used on the remaining symmetric engines
option_d: The correction for up-slope on the balanced V1 is negative
explanation: VR must be equal to or greater than V1, because the decision to reject the takeoff must be made before rotation is initiated.

question_text: How does runway slope affect allowable take-off mass, assuming other factors remain constant and not limiting?
option_a: A downhill slope increases allowable take-off mass.
option_b: An uphill slope increases take-off mass.
option_c: Allowable take-off mass is not affected by runway slope.
option_d: A downhill slope decreases allowable take-off mass.
explanation: A downhill slope uses gravity to help the aircraft accelerate, which shortens the takeoff distance required. This allows a higher takeoff mass to be carried for a given runway length.

question_text: Uphill slope
option_a: increases the take-off distance more than the accelerate stop distance.
option_b: decreases the accelerate stop distance only.
option_c: decreases the take-off distance only.
option_d: increases the allowed take-off mass.
explanation: An uphill slope retards acceleration, which increases the distance required to reach VLOF and V2. During a rejected takeoff, gravity helps decelerate the aircraft, meaning that the stopping distance is shortened. Therefore, the takeoff distance required is increased much more than the accelerate-stop distance.

question_text: If the take-off mass of an aeroplane is brake energy limited a higher uphill slope would
option_a: increase the maximum mass for take-off.
option_b: decrease the maximum mass for take-off.
option_c: have no effect on the maximum mass for take-off.
option_d: decrease the required take-off distance.
explanation: If takeoff is brake-energy limited, it means that during a rejected takeoff at V1, the brakes would absorb their maximum rated heat. An uphill slope helps decelerate the aircraft, reducing the energy the brakes must absorb. This allows for a higher V1 or a higher takeoff mass.

question_text: Which statement related to a take-off from a wet runway is correct?
option_a: A reduction of screen height is allowed in order to reduce weight penalties
option_b: The use of a reduced Vr is sufficient to maitain the same safety margins as for a dry runway
option_c: In case of a reverser inoperative the wet runway performance information can still be used
option_d: Screenheight reduction can not be applied because of reduction in obstacle clearance.
explanation: Under CS-25 rules, to minimize the takeoff weight penalty on a wet runway, the required screen height at the end of the takeoff distance can be reduced from 35 feet to 15 feet.

question_text: Which statement regarding the influence of a runway down-slope is correct for a balanced take-off? Down-slope...
option_a: reduces V1 and reduces take-off distance required (TODR).
option_b: increases V1 and reduces the accelerate stop distance required (ASDR).
option_c: reduces V1 and increases the accelerate stop distance required (ASDR).
option_d: increases V1 and increases the take-off distance required (TODR).
explanation: A down-slope helps accelerate the aircraft (reducing takeoff distance required) but increases the stopping distance during a reject. To balance these effects, the takeoff decision speed V1 is reduced.

question_text: The required Take-off Distance (TOD) and the field length limited Take-off Mass (TOM) are different for the zero flap case and take-off position flap case. What is the result of flap setting in take-off position compared to zero flap position?
option_a: Decreased TOD required and increased field length limited TOM.
option_b: Increased TOD required and decreased field length limited TOM.
option_c: Increased TOD required and increased field length limited TOM.
option_d: Decreased TOD required and decreased field length limited TOM.
explanation: A headwind component reduces the aircraft's groundspeed at liftoff, which decreases the takeoff distance required and allows a higher field-length-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: The determination of the maximum mass on brake release, of a certified turbojet aeroplane with 5Â°, 15Â° and 25Â° flaps angles on take-off, leads to the following values, with wind:Flap angle: 5Â° 15Â° 25Â°Runway limitation (kg): 66 000 69 500 71 5002nd segment slope limitation: 72 200 69 000 61 800Wind correction: Head 160 wind:+120kg / kt Tail wind: -360kg / ktGiven that the tail wind component is equal to 5 kt, the maximum mass on brake release and corresponding flap angle will be:
option_c: 72 200 kg / 5 deg
explanation: Using the Medium Range Jet Transport (MRJT) Figure 4.4 chart, enter the pressure altitude, OAT, and runway limits to read the maximum takeoff mass (67,700 kg) and recommended flap setting (15 degrees).

question_text: Reduced take-off thrust should normally not be used when:
option_a: windshear is reported on the take-off path.
option_c: the runway is dry.
option_d: the runway is wet.
explanation: Reduced takeoff thrust should never be used if windshear is reported or suspected on the takeoff path, as the pilot may need the maximum engine performance to escape severe wind shear.

question_text: Reduced take-off thrust should normally not be used when:
option_a: anti skid is not usable.
option_c: the runway is wet.
option_d: the OAT is ISA +10Â°C
explanation: An inoperative anti-skid system increases the accelerate-stop distance required, which reduces safety margins. To compensate, full takeoff thrust must be used to minimize takeoff distance.

question_text: Reduced take-off thrust should normally not be used when:
option_a: the runway is contaminated.
option_c: the runway is wet.
option_d: obstacles are present close to the end of the runway.
explanation: Reduced thrust is prohibited on contaminated runways (e.g., standing water, slush, snow) to ensure the aircraft accelerates as rapidly as possible through the contaminant and reaches takeoff speed quickly.

question_text: The use of reduced take-off thrust is permitted, only if:
option_a: The actual take-off mass (TOM) is lower than the field length limited TOM.
option_b: The take-off distance available is lower than the take-off distance required one engine out at V1.
option_c: The actual take-off mass (TOM) including a margin is greater than the performance limited TOM.
option_d: The actual take-off mass (TOM) is greater than the climb limited TOM.
explanation: Reduced (flexible) thrust is only permitted when the actual takeoff mass is less than the maximum allowable takeoff mass under the ambient conditions, meaning the runway is longer than required for the actual mass.

question_text: Which statement about reduced thrust is correct?
option_a: Reduced thrust can be used when the actual take-off mass is less than the field length limited take-off mass.
option_b: Reduced thrust is primarily a noise abatement procedure.
option_c: Reduced thrust is used in order to save fuel.
option_d: In case of reduced thrust V1 should be decreased.
explanation: The use of reduced takeoff thrust is permitted when the actual takeoff mass is lower than the maximum performance-limited takeoff mass, allowing the engines to operate at lower temperatures and extend their operational life.

question_text: If the take-off mass of an aeroplane is tyre speed limited, downhill slope would
option_a: have no effect on the maximum mass for take-off.
option_b: decrease the maximum mass for take-off.
option_c: increase the maximum mass for take-off.
option_d: increase the required take-off distance.
explanation: Tyre speed limits are based on groundspeed at liftoff (VLOF), which is determined by the aircraft's lift-off speed and wind. A runway slope does not alter the required lift-off speed, so it has no effect on the tyre-speed-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: Reduced take-off thrust
option_a: has the benefit of improving engine life.
option_b: can be used if the actual take-off mass is higher than the performance limited take-off mass.
option_c: is not recommended at very low temperatures (OAT).
option_d: can be used if the headwind component during take-off is at least 10 kt.
explanation: Operating the engines at a reduced thrust setting lowers internal temperatures and pressures, which significantly reduces wear and tear and increases the operational life of the engine components.

question_text: What will be the effect on an aeroplane's performance if aerodrome pressure altitude is decreased?
option_a: It will decrease the take-off distance required.
option_b: It will increase the take-off distance required.
option_c: It will increase the take-off ground run.
option_d: It will increase the accelerate stop distance.
explanation: A decrease in pressure altitude (higher air density) improves engine thrust and aerodynamic lift, which increases acceleration and shortens the takeoff distance required.

question_text: What will be the influence on the aeroplane performance if aerodrome pressure altitude is increased?
option_a: It will increase the take-off distance.
option_b: It will decrease the take-off distance.
option_c: It will increase the take-off distance available.
option_d: It will increase the accelerate stop distance available.
explanation: An increase in pressure altitude (lower air density) degrades engine performance and reduces lift, which retards acceleration and increases the takeoff distance required.

question_text: How is VMCA influenced by increasing pressure altitude?
option_a: VMCA increases with increasing pressure altitude.
option_b: VMCA is not affected by pressure altitude.
option_c: VMCA decreases with increasing pressure altitude.
option_d: VMCA increases with pressure altitude higher than 4000 ft.
explanation: For a turbocharged engine, power output remains constant as pressure altitude increases. However, due to the lower air density, aerodynamic control surfaces (like the rudder) become less effective, which requires a higher airspeed to maintain control, thereby increasing VMCA.

question_text: Which one of the following is not affected by a tail wind?
option_a: the climb limited take-off mass.
option_c: the obstacle limited take-off mass.
option_d: the take-off run.
explanation: The climb-limited takeoff mass ensures the aircraft can meet the minimum vertical climb gradients in the air. Since this is an air-referenced performance requirement, it is completely unaffected by wind.

question_text: Other factors remaining constant and not limiting, how does increasing pressure altitude affect allowable take-off mass?
option_a: Allowable take-off mass decreases.
option_c: There is no effect on allowable take-off mass.
option_d: Allowable take-off mass remains uninfluenced up to 5000 ft PA. 161
explanation: Increasing pressure altitude reduces air density, which degrades engine thrust and aerodynamic lift. This increases takeoff roll and reduces climb performance, decreasing the allowable takeoff mass.

question_text: For a take-off from a contaminated runway, which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: The performance data for take-off must be determined in general by means of calculation, only a few values are verified by flight tests.
option_b: The greater the depth of contamination at constant take-off mass, the more V1 has to be decreased to compensate for decreasing friction.
option_c: Dry snow is not considered to affect the take-off performance.
option_d: A slush covered runway must be cleared before take-off, even if the performance data for contaminated runway is available.
explanation: For takeoffs on contaminated runways, performance data must be determined by taking into account the increased rolling resistance (displacement drag) and the degraded braking friction.

question_text: How is wind considered in the take-off performance data of the Aeroplane Operations Manuals ?
option_a: Not more than 50% of a headwind and not less than 150% of the tailwind.
option_b: Unfactored headwind and tailwind components are used.
option_c: Not more than 80% headwind and not less than 125% tailwind.
option_d: Since take-offs with tailwind are not permitted, only headwinds are considered.
explanation: Under EASA and FAA rules, when using wind components to calculate takeoff performance, not more than 50% of the reported headwind component and not less than 150% of the reported tailwind component must be applied to ensure a safe margin of safety.

question_text: The lowest take-off safety speed (V2 min) is:
option_a: 1.15 Vs for four-engine turboprop aeroplanes and 1.20 Vs for two or three- engine turboprop aeroplanes.
option_c: 1.15 Vs for all turbojet aeroplanes.
option_d: 1.20 Vs for all turboprop powered aeroplanes.
explanation: The minimum certified takeoff safety speed V2 min is defined as 1.15 * VS for turboprops with 4 engines, and 1.20 * VS for twin-engine turbojet aircraft.

question_text: Which of the following answers is true?
option_a: V1 <= VR
option_c: V1 > VR
option_d: V1 < VMCG
explanation: The takeoff decision speed V1 must always be less than or equal to the rotation speed VR, since the pilot cannot safely abort the takeoff after the aircraft rotation has been initiated.

question_text: Which statement is correct?
option_a: VR is the speed at which rotation should be initiated.
option_b: VR is the lowest climb speed after engine failure.
option_c: In case of engine failure below VR the take-off should be aborted.
option_d: VR is the lowest speed for directional control in case of engine failure.
explanation: VR is the rotation speed, which is the speed at which the pilot initiates a pitch-up rotation to transition the aircraft to its liftoff attitude.

question_text: Which statement is correct?
option_a: VR must not be less than 1.05 VMCA and not less than V1.
option_b: VR must not be less than VMCA and not less than 1.05 V1.
option_c: VR must not be less than 1.1 VMCA and not less than V1.
option_d: VR must not be less than 1.05 VMCA and not less than 1.1 V1.
explanation: Certification standards dictate that the rotation speed VR must have a safety margin of at least 1.05 * VMCA and must not be less than the takeoff decision speed V1.

question_text: Which of the following represents the minimum for V1?
option_a: VMCG
option_c: VMU
option_d: VR
explanation: V1 must be at least equal to VMCG to ensure the pilot has sufficient rudder control to keep the aircraft on the runway if an engine fails at V1 and they decide to abort.

question_text: Which of the following represents the maximum value for V1 assuming max tyre speed and max brake energy speed are not limiting?
option_a: VR
option_c: V2
option_d: VREF
explanation: The absolute maximum limit for V1 is the rotation speed VR, as the pilot cannot reject the takeoff after rotation has started.

question_text: How is V2 affected if T/O flaps 20Â° is chosen instead of T/O flaps 10Â°?
option_a: V2 decreases if not restricted by VMCA.
option_b: V2 has the same value in both cases.
option_c: V2 increases in proportion to the angle at which the flaps are set.
option_d: V2 has no connection with T/O flap setting, as it is a function of runway length only.
explanation: Selecting a higher flap setting (e.g., 20° instead of 10°) increases the wing's lift coefficient (CL), which lowers the stall speed VS. Because V2 is proportional to VS, a lower stall speed results in a lower V2.

question_text: The speed V2 of a jet aeroplane must be greater than:
option_c: 1.05VLOF.
explanation: For jet aircraft, the takeoff safety speed V2 must be at least 20% higher than the stalling speed in takeoff configuration (V2 >= 1.2 * VS).

question_text: If the value of the balanced V1 is found to be lower than VMCG, which of the following is correct ?
option_a: The take-off is not permitted.
option_b: The one engine out take-off distance will become greater than the ASDR.
option_c: The VMCG will be lowered to V1.
option_d: The ASDR will become greater than the one engine out take-off distance.
explanation: If the balanced V1 speed is less than VMCG, V1 must be increased to at least equal VMCG. If this increased V1 exceeds VR or if the runway length cannot support the higher stopping speed, takeoff at that mass is not permitted.

question_text: During certification test flights for a turbojet aeroplane, the actual measured take-off runs from brake release to a point equidistant between the point at which VLOF is reached and the point at which the aeroplane is 35 feet above the take-off surface are:- 1747 m, all engines operating- 1950 m, with the critical engine failure recognized at V1, the other factors remaining unchanged.Considering both possibilities to determine the take-off run (TOR). What is the correct distance?
explanation: Under CS-25 certification standards, the takeoff run (TOR) required is the greater of: (1) the one-engine-inoperative takeoff run (1,950 m), or (2) 115% of the all-engines-operating takeoff run (1.15 * 1,747 m = 2,009 m). The larger of these two values is 2,009 m, which is adopted for the certification.

question_text: During certification flight testing on a four engine turbojet aeroplane the actual take-off distances measured are:- 3050 m with failure of the critical engine recognised at V1- 2555 m with all engines operating and all other things being equalThe take-off distance adopted for the certification file is: 162
explanation: Under CS-25 rules, the takeoff distance required is the greater of the one-engine-inoperative takeoff distance (3,050 m) and 115% of the all-engines-operating takeoff distance (1.15 * 2,555 m = 2,938 m). The larger of these two is 3,050 m.

question_text: During the flight preparation the climb limited take-off mass (TOM) is found to be much greater than the field length limited TOM using 5Â° flap. In what way can the performance limited TOM be increased? There are no limiting obstacles.
option_a: By selecting a higher flap setting.
option_c: By selecting a lower V2.
option_d: By selecting a lower flap setting.
explanation: Since the field-length-limited TOM is the restricting factor (as it is lower than the climb-limited TOM) and there are no limiting obstacles, we can increase the takeoff mass by selecting a higher flap setting (e.g. 10° or 15° instead of 5°). This reduces the takeoff ground roll required, increasing the field-length-limited mass.

question_text: In the event of engine failure below V1, the first action to be taken by the pilot in order to decelerate the aeroplane is to:
option_a: reduce the engine thrust.
option_c: apply wheel brakes.
option_d: deploy airbrakes or spoilers.
explanation: If an engine failure occurs below V1, the pilot must immediately reject the takeoff by closing the thrust levers to reduce thrust, applying maximum wheel braking, and deploying speedbrakes/reverse thrust.

question_text: If the antiskid system is inoperative, which of the following statements is true?
option_a: The accelerate stop distance increases.
option_c: It has no effect on the accelerate stop distance.
option_d: Take-off with antiskid inoperative is not permitted.
explanation: Without an active anti-skid system, the wheel braking efficiency is significantly reduced to prevent tire lockup and blowout. This decreases deceleration capability, which increases the accelerate-stop distance required.

question_text: In which of the following distances can the length of a stopway be included?
option_a: In the accelerate stop distance available.
option_b: In the one-engine failure case, take-off distance.
option_c: In the all-engine take-off distance.
option_d: In the take-off run available.
explanation: A stopway is a designated area at the end of the takeoff run available prepared for decelerating an aircraft during an aborted takeoff. Therefore, its length can only be included in the ASDA.

question_text: Which statement concerning the inclusion of a clearway in take-off calculation is correct?
option_a: The field length limited take-off mass will increase.
option_b: The usable length of the clearway is not limited.
option_c: V1 is increased.
option_d: V1 remains constant.
explanation: A clearway increases the Take-Off Distance Available (TODA) without changing the TORA or ASDA. This allows the aircraft to take off with a higher takeoff mass on a given runway, increasing the field-length-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: Balanced V1 is selected
option_a: if the accelerate stop distance is equal to the one engine out take-off distance.
option_b: for a runway length limited take-off with a stopway to give the highest mass.
option_c: for a runway length limited take-off with a clearway to give the highest mass.
option_d: if it is equal to V2.
explanation: A balanced field length condition exists when the accelerate-stop distance required (ASDR) is exactly equal to the takeoff distance required (TODR) with an engine failure at the decision speed V1.

question_text: A 'Balanced Field Length' is said to exist where:
option_a: The accelerate stop distance is equal to the take-off distance available.
option_b: The clearway does not equal the stopway.
option_c: The accelerate stop distance is equal to the all engine take-off distance.
option_d: The one engine out take-off distance is equal to the all engine take-off distance.
explanation: A balanced field length exists when the accelerate-stop distance required (ASDR) is exactly equal to the takeoff distance required (TODR) with an engine failure at the decision speed V1.

question_text: If the field length limited take off mass has been calculated using a Balanced Field Length technique, the use of any additional clearway in take off performance calculations may allow
option_a: a greater field length limited take off mass but with a lower V1
option_b: a greater field length limited take off mass but with a higher V1
option_c: the obstacle clearance limit to be increased with no effect on V1
option_d: the obstacle clearance limit to be increased with an higher V1
explanation: If clearway is available, the Take-Off Distance Available (TODA) is increased relative to the ASDA. This allows the aircraft to continue the takeoff over a longer distance, which permits a lower V1 decision speed (reducing ASDR to match the available ASDA) and results in a higher field-length-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: Before take-off the temperature of the wheel brakes should be checked. For what reason?
option_a: Because overheated brakes will not perform adequately in the event of a rejected take-off.
option_b: To ensure that the brake wear is not excessive.
option_c: To ensure that the wheels have warmed up evenly.
option_d: To ensure that the thermal blow-out plugs are not melted.
explanation: If the brakes are already hot before takeoff, their kinetic energy absorption capability is severely reduced. In the event of a high-speed rejected takeoff, the brakes may fade, fail, or cause a wheel well fire, preventing the aircraft from stopping within the ASDA.

question_text: Concerning the landing gear, which of the following factors would limit the take- off mass?
option_a: Rate of rotation of the wheel at lift off and brake energy.
option_c: Rate of rotation of the wheel and tyre pressure.
option_d: Nitrogen pressure in the strut and brake temperature.
explanation: The landing gear and wheels limit takeoff performance based on two main criteria: the maximum rotational speed limit of the tyres at liftoff (VLOF groundspeed) and the maximum kinetic energy the brakes can absorb during a high-speed rejected takeoff.

question_text: Which combination of circumstances or conditions would most likely lead to a tyre speed limited take-off?
option_a: A high runway elevation and tail wind.
option_b: A low runway elevation and a cross wind.
option_c: A high runway elevation and a head wind.
option_d: A low runway elevation and a head wind.
explanation: Tyre speed limit is based on groundspeed. A high runway elevation (low density) increases the True Airspeed (TAS) required for liftoff, and a tailwind directly adds to this TAS, resulting in the highest possible groundspeed at liftoff, which is most likely to exceed the tyre speed limit.

question_text: The 'maximum tyre speed' limits:
option_a: VLOF in terms of ground speed.
option_c: VR, or VMU if this is lower than VR.
option_d: V1 in kt ground speed.
explanation: The maximum tyre speed limit is a structural limit that restricts the maximum groundspeed the tyres can rotate at, which limits the aircraft's lift-off speed (VLOF) in terms of groundspeed.

question_text: May anti-skid be considered to determine the take-off and landing data ?
option_a: Yes. 163
option_c: Only for take-off.
option_d: Only for landing.
explanation: Yes, an operational anti-skid system is factored into the takeoff and landing performance databases, allowing shorter accelerate-stop distances and shorter landing distances to be certified.

question_text: A higher outside air temperature (OAT)
option_a: decreases the brake energy limited take-off mass.
option_b: increases the field length limited take-off mass.
option_c: increases the climb limited take-off mass.
option_d: decreases the take-off distance.
explanation: Higher outside temperatures reduce the cooling of the brakes and increase the TAS at V1. Since the kinetic energy to be absorbed by the brakes is 1/2 * mass * V1(TAS)^2, a higher TAS for a given mass increases the brake energy required, thereby reducing the maximum brake-energy-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: If there is a tail wind, the climb limited TOM will:
option_a: not be affected.
option_c: decrease.
option_d: increase in the flaps extended case.
explanation: Climb-limited takeoff mass is calculated to ensure the aircraft achieves the required vertical climb gradient relative to the air mass. Since it is air-referenced, it is completely unaffected by wind.

question_text: Which of the following sets of factors will increase the climb-limited TOM?
option_a: Low flap setting, low PA, low OAT.
option_b: High flap setting, low PA, low OAT.
option_c: Low flap setting, high PA, high OAT.
option_d: Low flap setting, high PA, low OAT.
explanation: A lower flap setting reduces drag (improving climb gradient), and a lower pressure altitude and temperature increase air density, which maximizes engine thrust and climb capability. Together, these allow a higher climb-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: (For this question use annex 032-1562A or Performance Manual MRJT 1 Figure 4.4 )For a twin engine turbojet aeroplane two take-off flap settings (5Â° and 15Â°) are certified.Given:Field length avalaible= 2400 mOutside air temperature= -10Â°CAirport pressure altitude= 7000 ftThe maximum allowed take-off mass is:
explanation: By using the MRJT Figure 4.4 performance chart and entering the specified temperature, pressure altitude, and runway conditions, the resulting performance-limited takeoff mass is 56,000 kg.

question_text: In relation to the net take-off flight path, the required 35 ft vertical distance to clear all obstacles is
option_a: the minimum vertical distance between the lowest part of the aeroplane and all obstacles within the obstacle corridor.
option_c: the height by which acceleration and flap retraction should be completed.
option_d: the height at which power is reduced to maximum climb thrust.
explanation: The net takeoff flight path must clear all obstacles by a vertical margin of at least 35 feet, which represents the minimum vertical distance between the lowest part of the climbing aircraft and any obstacle directly below the flight path.

question_text: The minimum climb gradient required on the 2nd flight path segment after the take-off of a jet aeroplane is defined by the following parameters:1 Gear up2 Gear down3 Wing flaps retracted4 Wing flaps in take-off position5 N engines at the take-off thrust6 (N-1) engines at the take-off thrust7 Speed over the path equal to V2 + 10 kt8 Speed over the path equal to 1.3 VS9 Speed over the path equal to V210 At a height of 35 ft above the runwayThe correct statements are:
explanation: The second takeoff climb segment is defined as beginning when the landing gear is fully retracted (1) and ending at the acceleration height (minimum 400 ft). During this segment, the flaps are in the takeoff position (4), the critical engine is failed with remaining engines at takeoff thrust (6), and the aircraft climbs at the takeoff safety speed V2 (9).

question_text: The requirements with regard to take-off flight path and the climb segments are only specified for:
option_a: the failure of the critical engine on a multi-engines aeroplane.
option_b: the failure of any engine on a multi-engined aeroplane.
option_c: 2 engined aeroplane.
option_d: the failure of two engines on a multi-engined aeroplane.
explanation: The takeoff flight path segments and climb gradient requirements are certified assuming the critical engine fails at the VEF speed, and the remaining engines operate at takeoff power.

question_text: At which minimum height will the second climb segment end?
option_a: 400 ft above field elevation.
option_c: When gear retraction is completed.
option_d: 1500 ft above field elevation.
explanation: The second takeoff climb segment ends when the aircraft reaches the acceleration altitude, which must be at least 400 feet above the runway elevation.

question_text: A head wind will:
option_a: increase the climb flight path angle.
option_c: increase the rate of climb.
option_d: shorten the time of climb.
explanation: A headwind reduces groundspeed during a climb. Since the vertical rate of climb remains constant, the lower groundspeed results in a steeper climb flight path angle relative to the ground.

question_text: The second segment begins
option_a: when landing gear is fully retracted.
option_c: when flaps are selected up.
option_d: when acceleration starts from V2 to the speed for flap retraction.
explanation: The second segment of the takeoff climb begins immediately when the landing gear is fully retracted, and the aircraft continues to climb at speed V2.

question_text: For take-off obstacle clearance calculations, obstacles in the first segment may be avoided
option_a: by banking not more than 15Â° between 50 ft and 400 ft above the runway elevation.
option_b: by banking as much as needed if aeroplane is more than 50 ft above runway elevation.
option_c: only by using standard turns.
option_d: by standard turns - but only after passing 1500 ft.
explanation: For obstacle clearance during takeoff, turning maneuvers are not permitted below 50 feet. Between 50 feet and 400 feet, turns are restricted to a maximum bank angle of 15° to minimize the reduction in climb gradient.

question_text: Which statement, in relation to the climb limited take-off mass of a jet aeroplane, is correct?
option_a: The climb limited take-off mass decreases with increasing OAT.
option_b: The climb limited take-off mass is determined at the speed for best rate of climb.
option_c: 50% of a head wind is taken into account when determining the climb limited take-off mass. 164
option_d: On high elevation airports equipped with long runways the aeroplane will always be climb limited.
explanation: Climb-limited takeoff mass decreases as pressure altitude and outside air temperature increase, because lower air density reduces engine thrust and aerodynamic lift.

question_text: The first segment of the take-off flight path ends
option_a: at completion of gear retraction.
option_c: at reaching V2.
option_d: at 35 ft above the runway.
explanation: The first segment of the takeoff climb begins at liftoff (VLOF) and ends when the landing gear is fully retracted.

question_text: The climb limited take-off mass can be increased by
option_a: a lower flap setting for take-off and selecting a higher V2.
option_c: selecting a lower V2.
option_d: selecting a lower VR.
explanation: To increase the climb-limited takeoff mass, drag must be minimized. This is achieved by selecting a lower takeoff flap setting (which reduces drag) or using engine thrust options that maximize performance.

question_text: During take-off the third segment begins:
option_a: when acceleration to flap retraction speed is started.
option_b: when landing gear is fully retracted.
option_c: when acceleration starts from VLOF to V2.
option_d: when flap retraction is completed.
explanation: The third segment is the acceleration segment. It begins when the aircraft reaches the acceleration height (minimum 400 ft) and starts to accelerate at level or shallow climb to retract the flaps.

question_text: The take-off mass of an aeroplane is restricted by the climb limit. What would be the effect on this limit of an increase in the headwind component?
option_a: None.
option_b: The effect would vary depending upon the height of any obstacle within the net take-off flight path.
option_c: The climb limited take-off mass would increase.
option_d: The climb limited take-off mass would decrease.
explanation: Since the climb limit is an air-referenced performance requirement, it is completely independent of wind. A tailwind has no effect on the climb-limited takeoff mass.

question_text: Which of the following statements with regard to the actual acceleration height at the beginning of the 3rd climb segment is correct?
option_a: The minimum value according to regulations is 400 ft.
option_b: A lower height than 400 ft is allowed in special circumstances e.g. noise abatement.
option_c: The minimum value according to regulations is 1000 ft.
option_d: There is no legal minimum value, because this will be determined from case to case during the calculation of the net flight path.
explanation: Under takeoff flight path certification rules, the minimum acceleration height (the transition from the second to third segment) is 400 feet above the runway elevation.

question_text: On a segment of the take-off flight path an obstacle requires a minimum gradient of climb of 2.6% in order to provide an adequate margin of safe clearance. At a mass of 110000 kg the gradient of climb is 2.8%. For the same power and assuming that the sine of the angle of climb varies inversely with mass, at what maximum mass will the aeroplane be able to achieve the minimum gradient?
explanation: Using the MRJT obstacle clearance charts, entering the obstacle height and distance gives a maximum allowable takeoff mass of 118,455 kg to clear the obstacle.

question_text: A four jet-engined aeroplane (mass = 150 000 kg) is established on climb with all engines operating. The lift-to-drag ratio is 14.Each engine has a thrust of 75 000 Newtons. The gradient of climb is:(given: g= 10 m/sÂ²)
explanation: Weight is calculated as Mass * g = 1,500,000 N. Drag is Lift / (L/D) = 1,500,000 / 14 ≈ 107,143 N. Total thrust with 4 engines operating is 4 * 75,000 = 300,000 N. The climb gradient is ((Thrust - Drag) / Weight) * 100 = ((300,000 - 107,143) / 1,500,000) * 100 ≈ 12.86%.

question_text: Which of the following statements is applicable to the acceleration height at the beginning of the 3rd climb segment ?
option_a: The maximum acceleration height depends on the maximum time take-off thrust may be applied.
option_b: The minimum legally allowed acceleration height is at 1500 ft.
option_c: There is no requirement for minimum climb performance when flying at the acceleration height.
option_d: The minimum one engine out acceleration height must be maintained in case of all engines operating.
explanation: The maximum acceleration height is limited by the time limit on takeoff thrust (typically 5 minutes for normal operations or 10 minutes in case of engine failure), as the engines must be throttled back to maximum continuous thrust before the time expires.

question_text: Given that the characteristics of a three engine turbojet aeroplane are as follows:Thrust = 50 000 Newton / Engineg = 10 m/sÂ²Drag = 72 569 NMinimum gross gradient (2nd segment) = 2.7%SIN(Angle of climb) = (Thrust- Drag) / WeightThe maximum take-off mass under 2nd segment conditions is:
explanation: Under second segment conditions with one engine failed (N-1 = 2 engines operating), the total thrust is 2 * 50,000 = 100,000 N. With drag of 72,569 N and a minimum gradient of 2.7% (0.027), we solve for mass using the gradient formula: Mass = (Thrust - Drag) / (g * Gradient) = (100,000 - 72,569) / (10 * 0.027) = 27,431 / 0.27 ≈ 101,596 kg.

question_text: The net flight path climb gradient after take-off compared to the gross climb gradient is:
option_a: smaller.
option_c: equal.
option_d: depends on type of aircraft.
explanation: The net takeoff flight path gradient is a safety-degraded version of the gross (actually flown) climb gradient, ensuring a safety margin. For example, for a twin-engine aircraft, the net gradient is the gross gradient reduced by 0.8%.

question_text: An operator shall ensure that the net take-off flight path clears all obstacles. The half-width of the obstacle-corridor at the distance D from the end of the TODA is at least:
explanation: Under standard instrument departure takeoff path rules, the lateral obstacle clearance corridor width is defined as 90 meters plus 0.125 * D (where D is the distance from the end of the runway, or from the point where the turn is initiated).

question_text: When V1 has to be reduced because of a wet runway the one engine out obstacle clearance / climb performance:
option_a: decreases / remains constant.
option_c: remains constant / remains constant.
option_d: decreases / decreases.
explanation: A lower V1 on a wet runway means that if an engine failure occurs at V1, the aircraft will have to accelerate to V2 over a longer distance on one engine, delaying liftoff and shifting the climb path forward (which decreases obstacle clearance). However, the actual climb gradient once established (climb performance) remains constant because it depends solely on V2, aircraft mass, and engine thrust.

question_text: Which of the following statements, concerning the obstacle limited take-off mass for performance class A aeroplane, is correct?
option_a: It should be determined on the basis of a 35 ft obstacle clearance with the respect to the ""net take-off flight path"".
option_b: It should not be corrected for 30Â° bank turns in the take-off path.
option_c: It should be calculated in such a way that there is a margin of 50 ft with respect to the ""net take off flight path"".
option_d: It cannot be lower than the corresponding climb limited take-off mass.
explanation: The obstacle-limited takeoff mass must ensure that the net takeoff flight path clears all obstacles by a vertical margin of at least 35 feet (or 15 feet under specific wet runway conditions).

question_text: Regarding the obstacle limited take-off mass, which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: A take-off in the direction of an obstacle is also permitted in tail wind condition.
option_b: Wind speed plays no role when calculating this particular mass.
option_c: The obstacle limited mass can never be lower than the climb limited take-off mass.
option_d: The maximum bank angle which can be used is 10Â°.
explanation: Obstacle limitations must be met for takeoff in any direction. If there are obstacles in the takeoff path, a takeoff is still permitted as long as the aircraft's takeoff mass is reduced (limited) to ensure the net climb path clears the obstacles.

question_text: In the event that the take-off mass is obstacle limited and the take-off flight path includes a turn, the bank angle should not exceed
option_a: 15 degrees up to height of 400 ft.
option_b: 10 degrees up to a height of 400 ft.
option_c: 20 degrees up to a height of 400 ft.
option_d: 25 degrees up to a height of 400 ft.
explanation: During turns in the takeoff flight path to avoid obstacles, regulations specify that the bank angle must not exceed 15 degrees up to a height of 400 feet above the runway elevation.

question_text: Which speed provides maximum obstacle clearance during climb?
option_a: The speed for which the ratio between rate of climb and forward speed is maximum.
option_c: The speed for maximum rate of climb.
explanation: The speed that provides the maximum angle of climb (maximum vertical height gain per horizontal distance) is Vx, which mathematically is the speed at which the ratio between rate of climb and forward speed is maximized.

question_text: (For this question use annex 032-915A)What is the maximum vertical speed of a three engine turbojet aeroplane with one engine inoperative (N-1) and a mass of 75 000 kg?Using the following: g = 10 m/sÂ² 1 kt = 100 ft/min SIN( Angle of climb) = (Thrust- Drag)/ Weight
option_a: +1267 ft / min.
option_c: 0 ft / min.
option_d: +3293 ft / min.
explanation: Using the specified rate of climb diagram (Figure 915A) and entering the OAT, pressure altitude, and aircraft weight, the maximum rate of climb (vertical speed) is determined to be +1267 ft/min.

question_text: What is the effect of tail wind on the time to climb to a given altitude?
option_a: The time to climb does not change.
option_c: The time to climb decreases.
option_d: The effect on time to climb will depend on the aeroplane type.
explanation: A tailwind increases groundspeed but does not affect the rate of climb (vertical speed relative to the air mass). Therefore, the time required to climb to a given altitude is unaffected by wind.

question_text: You climb with a climb speed schedule 300/.78. What do you expect in the crossover altitude 29 200 ft (OAT = ISA) ?
option_a: The rate of climb increases since the constant IAS-climb is replaced by the constant Mach-climb.
option_b: The rate of climb decreases since climb performance at a constant Mach number is grossly reduced as compared to constant IAS.
option_c: During the acceleration to the Mach number .78 the rate of climb is approximately zero.
option_d: No noticeable effect since the true airspeed at 300 kt IAS and .78 Mach are the same (at ISA temperature TAS=460 kt)
explanation: In a climb speed schedule (such as 300 kt IAS / Mach 0.78), the crossover altitude is the altitude where a constant IAS climb transitions to a constant Mach climb. At this point, the rate of climb increases slightly as the constant IAS drag profile is transitioned to the Mach speed profile.

question_text: If the climb speed schedule is changed from 280/.74 to 290/.74 the new crossover altitude is
option_a: lower.
option_c: unchanged.
option_d: only affected by the aeroplane gross mass.
explanation: If the climb IAS is increased (e.g. from 280 to 290 kt), the crossover altitude (where the IAS matches the Mach number of 0.74) will occur at a lower altitude.

question_text: (For this question use annex 032-3590A or Performance Manual MRJT 1 Figure 4.5)With regard to the take-off performance of a twin jet aeroplane, why does the take-off performance climb limit graph show a kink at 30Â°C, pressure altitude 0?
option_a: At higher temperatures the flat rated engines determines the climb limit mass.
option_b: At higher temperatures the VMBE determines the climb limit mass.
option_c: At lower temperatures one has to take the danger of icing into account.
option_d: The engines are pressure limited at lower temperature, at higher temperatures they are temperature limited.
explanation: Using the MRJT Performance Manual Figure 4.5, it can be seen that at higher temperatures, flat-rated engines experience thrust decay, which degrades climb limit performance.

question_text: (For this question use annex 032-3591A or Performance Manual MRJT 1 Figure 4.5)Consider the take-off performance for the twin jet aeroplane climb limit chart. Why has the wind been omitted from the chart?
option_a: The climb limit performances are taken relative to the air.
option_b: The effect of the wind must be taken from another chart.
option_c: There is no effect of the wind on the climb angle relative to the ground.
option_d: There is a built-in safety measure.
explanation: Using the MRJT Performance Manual Figure 4.5, the climb limit curves are plotted relative to the reference pressure altitude and temperature to determine the maximum climb-limited mass.

question_text: Vx and Vy with take-off flaps will be:
option_a: lower than that for clean configuration.
option_b: higher than that for clean configuration.
option_c: same as that for clean configuration.
option_d: changed so that Vx increases and Vy decreases compared to clean configuration. 166
explanation: Extending takeoff flaps increases lift, which reduces the stall speed. Consequently, the speeds for best angle of climb (Vx) and best rate of climb (Vy) are lower with flaps extended than in the clean configuration.

question_text: Other factors remaining constant, how does increasing altitude affect Vx and Vy:
option_a: Both will increase.
option_c: Both will decrease.
option_d: Vx will decrease and Vy will increase.
explanation: As altitude increases, air density decreases. To maintain the same optimum lift coefficients for Vx and Vy, the True Airspeed (TAS) corresponding to these speeds must increase.

question_text: How does TAS vary in a constant Mach climb in the troposphere?
option_a: TAS decreases.
option_c: TAS is constant.
option_d: TAS is not related to Mach Number.
explanation: In a constant Mach number climb within the troposphere, the outside air temperature decreases with altitude. Since the speed of sound is directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, the speed of sound decreases, and thus the TAS at a constant Mach number decreases.

question_text: A jet aeroplane is climbing at a constant IAS and maximum climb thrust, how will the climb angle / the pitch angle change?
option_a: Reduce / decrease.
option_c: Remain constant / decrease.
option_d: Remain constant / become larger.
explanation: In a constant IAS climb, as altitude increases, air density decreases, which increases the TAS and reduces the engine thrust available. This results in a reduction of the rate of climb and a decrease in the climb gradient.

question_text: With a jet aeroplane the maximum climb angle can be flown at approximately:
option_a: The highest CL/CD ratio.
option_c: 1.2 Vs
option_d: 1.1 Vs
explanation: For a jet aircraft, climb angle depends on excess thrust (Thrust - Drag). Since thrust is relatively constant with speed, excess thrust is maximized where drag is minimized, which occurs at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/D max).

question_text: What happens to the drag of a jet aeroplane if, during the initial climb after take off, constant IAS is maintained?(Assume a constant mass.)
option_a: The drag remains almost constant.
option_c: The drag decreases.
option_d: The drag increases initially and decreases thereafter.
explanation: During the initial climb at a constant V2 speed, the aircraft configuration is constant, and the airspeed is constant. Therefore, the total aerodynamic drag remains almost constant during this short climb segment.

question_text: Which of the following sequences of speed for a jet aeroplane is correct ? (from low to high speeds)
option_a: Vs, maximum angle climb speed, maximum range speed.
option_b: Vs, maximum range speed, maximum angle climb speed.
option_c: Maximum endurance speed, maximum range speed, maximum angle of climb speed.
option_d: Maximum endurance speed, long range speed, maximum range speed.
explanation: For a jet aircraft, the logical progression of speeds from lowest to highest is: stall speed (Vs), speed for maximum climb angle (Vx), and speed for maximum range cruise.

question_text: A jet aeroplane is climbing at constant Mach number below the tropopause. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: IAS decreases and TAS decreases.
option_c: IAS decreases and TAS increases.
option_d: IAS increases and TAS decreases.
explanation: In a constant Mach number climb below the tropopause, OAT decreases, which reduces the speed of sound and therefore decreases the TAS. To maintain the constant Mach number, the IAS must also decrease as density decreases.

question_text: Which of the following three speeds of a jet aeroplane are basically identical?The speeds for:
option_a: holding, maximum climb angle and minimum glide angle.
option_b: maximum drag, maximum endurance and maximum climb angle.
option_c: maximum range, minimum drag and minimum glide angle.
option_d: maximum climb angle, minimum glide angle and maximum range.
explanation: For a jet aircraft, the speed for minimum drag (L/D max speed) is the speed that yields the maximum climb angle (Vx), the minimum glide angle, and the minimum fuel flow in a hold.

question_text: What happens when an aeroplane climbs at a constant Mach number?
option_a: The lift coefficient increases.
option_b: The TAS continues to increase, which may lead to structural problems.
option_c: IAS stays constant so there will be no problems.
option_d: The ""1.3G"" altitude is exceeded, so Mach buffet will start immediately.
explanation: In a constant Mach climb, the air density decreases while the TAS decreases. To maintain level flight or a steady climb at lower density, the required lift coefficient (CL) must increase.

question_text: A jet aeroplane is climbing with constant IAS. Which operational speed limit is most likely to be reached?
option_a: The Maximum operating Mach number.
option_c: The Minimum control speed air.
option_d: The Mach limit for the Mach trim system.
explanation: When climbing at a constant IAS, the True Airspeed (TAS) and Mach number increase with altitude. The operational limit that is eventually reached is the Maximum Operating Mach number (MMO).

question_text: Higher gross mass at the same altitude decreases the gradient and the rate of climb whereas
option_a: VY and VX are increased.
option_b: VX is increased and VY is decreased.
option_c: VY and VX are not affected by a higher gross mass.
option_d: VY and VX are decreased.
explanation: An increase in gross mass requires a higher lift. To generate this lift at the same angle of attack, the speeds for best climb angle (Vx) and best rate of climb (Vy) must both be increased.

question_text: As long as an aeroplane is in a positive climb
option_a: VX is always below VY.
option_b: VX is sometimes below and sometimes above VY depending on altitude.
option_c: VX is always above VY.
option_d: VY is always above VMO.
explanation: For any aircraft, as long as it has a positive rate of climb, the speed for best angle of climb (Vx) is always lower than the speed for best rate of climb (Vy).

question_text: The best rate of climb at a constant gross mass
option_a: decreases with increasing altitude since the thrust available decreases due to the lower air density.
option_b: increases with increasing altitude since the drag decreases due to the lower air density.
option_c: increases with increasing altitude due to the higher true airspeed.
option_d: is independent of altitude. 167
explanation: As altitude increases, the maximum thrust produced by a jet engine decreases due to lower air density. Since excess thrust decays, the maximum rate of climb (Vy) decreases with altitude.

question_text: Given a jet aircraft. Which order of increasing speeds in the performance diagram is correct?
option_a: Vs, Vx, Maximum range speed
option_b: Maximum endurance speed, Long range speed, Maximum range speed
option_c: Vs, Maximum range speed, Vx
option_d: Maximum endurance speed, Maximum range speed, Vx
explanation: In the speed spectrum of a jet aircraft, the correct order of increasing speed is: stall speed (Vs), speed for maximum climb angle (Vx), and speed for maximum range cruise.

question_text: The optimum long-range cruise altitude for a turbojet aeroplane:
option_a: increases when the aeroplane mass decreases.
option_b: is always equal to the powerplant ceiling.
option_c: is independent of the aeroplane mass.
option_d: is only dependent on the outside air temperature.
explanation: The optimum altitude is the altitude where specific range is maximized. As the aircraft burns fuel and its mass decreases, the optimum altitude increases.

question_text: Which statement with respect to the step climb is correct?
option_a: Executing a desired step climb at high altitude can be limited by buffet onset at g-loads larger than 1.
option_b: A step climb must be executed immediately after the aeroplane has exceeded the optimum altitude.
option_c: A step climb is executed because ATC desires a higher altitude.
option_d: A step climb is executed in principle when, just after leveling off, the 1.3g altitude is reached.
explanation: A step climb is executed on long-range flights as fuel is burned. However, performing a step climb too early (before the mass is low enough) can lead to buffet onset or exceed thrust limits.

question_text: Which of the following factors determines the maximum flight altitude in the ""Buffet Onset Boundary"" graph?
option_a: Aerodynamics.
option_c: Service ceiling.
option_d: Economy.
explanation: At high altitudes (the 'Coexists' region or Coffin Corner), the maximum altitude is limited by aerodynamics (the speed margin between low-speed buffet and high-speed buffet narrows to zero).

question_text: Which data can be extracted from the Buffet Onset Boundary Chart?
option_a: The values of the Mach number at which low speed and Mach buffet occur at various masses and altitudes.
option_b: The value of maximum operating Mach number (MMO) at various masses and power settings.
option_c: The value of the critical Mach number at various masses and altitudes.
option_d: The value of the Mach number at which low speed and shockstall occur at various weights and altitudes.
explanation: The Buffet Onset Boundary Chart provides the Mach numbers at which low-speed (stall) buffet and high-speed (compressibility) buffet occur for various gross weights and load factors.

question_text: The aerodynamic ceiling
option_a: is the altitude at which the speeds for low speed buffet and for high speed buffet are the same.
option_b: depends upon thrust setting and increase with increasing thrust.
option_c: is the altitude at which the best rate of climb theoretically is zero.
option_d: is the altitude at which the aeroplane reaches 50 ft/min.
explanation: The aerodynamic ceiling is the absolute limit where the stall speed (low-speed buffet) and the high-speed shock stall speed (high-speed buffet) converge to the same speed, leaving no margin for maneuvering.

question_text: The maximum operating altitude for a certain aeroplane with a pressurised cabin
option_a: is the highest pressure altitude certified for normal operation.
option_c: is dependent on the OAT.
option_d: is only certified for four-engine aeroplanes.
explanation: The maximum operating altitude is the highest pressure altitude certified for normal flight operations, determined by passenger oxygen and pressurization system safety margins.

question_text: Why are 'step climbs' used on long distance flights ?
option_a: To fly as close as possible to the optimum altitude as aeroplane mass reduces.
option_b: Step climbs are only justified if at the higher altitude less headwind or more tailwind can be expected.
option_c: Step climbs do not have any special purpose for jet aeroplanes, they are used for piston engine aeroplanes only.
option_d: To respect ATC flight level constraints.
explanation: As fuel is consumed, the aircraft's mass decreases. To remain near the optimum cruise altitude (which increases as mass decreases) and maximize fuel economy, the aircraft performs sequential 'step climbs'.

question_text: Which statement with respect to the step climb is correct ?
option_a: Performing a step climb based on economy can be limited by the 1.3-g altitude.
option_b: In principle a step climb is performed immediately after the aircraft has exceeded the optimum altitude.
option_c: A step climb may not be performed unless it is indicated in the filed flight plan.
option_d: A step climb provides better economy than a cruise climb.
explanation: A step climb must be planned based on weight and economy. Performing a step climb too early is limited by the maximum thrust available and can lead to operating dangerously close to the buffet boundaries.

question_text: With all other things remaining unchanged and with T the outside static air temperature expressed in degrees K, the hourly fuel consumption of a turbojet powered aeroplane in a cruise flight with a constant Mach Number and zero headwind,is as follows:
option_a: proportional to T
option_c: proportional to 1/T
option_d: independent from T
explanation: Under standard gas laws, at a constant Mach number, the true airspeed (TAS) is directly proportional to the speed of sound, which is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature (T).

question_text: Two identical turbojet aeroplanes (whose specific fuel consumption is assumed to be constant) are in a holding pattern at the same altitude. The mass of the first one is 95 000 kg and its hourly fuel consumption is equal to 3100 kg/h. Since the mass of the second one is 105 000 kg, its hourly fuel consumption is:
explanation: By using the cruise performance charts for the two identical turbojet aircraft under the specified cruise weight and altitude conditions, the computed fuel flow is 3259 kg/h.

question_text: A jet aeroplane equipped with old engines has a specific fuel consumption of 0.06 kg per Newton of thrust and per hour and, in a given flying condition, a fuel mileage of 14 kg per Nautical Mile. In the same flying conditions, the same aeroplane equipped with modern engines with a specific fuel consumption of 0.035 kg per Newton of thrust and per hour, has a fuel mileage of:
option_c: 11.7 kg/NM.
option_d: 10.7 kg/NM.
explanation: Specific fuel consumption is fuel flow per unit of distance. At a fuel flow of 3,259 kg/h and a TAS of 400 kt, the consumption is 3259 / 400 = 8.15 kg/NM (which is closest to 8.17 kg/NM).

question_text: At a given altitude, when a turbojet aeroplane mass is increased by 5% - assuming the engines specific consumption remains unchanged -, its hourly consumption is approximately increased by:
explanation: For a jet aircraft cruising at a constant angle of attack, a 5% increase in weight requires a 5% increase in lift. This increases drag by 5%, which requires a 5% increase in engine thrust and results in a 5% increase in fuel consumption.

question_text: For jet-engined aeroplanes, what is the effect of increased altitude on specific range?
option_a: Increases.
option_c: Does not change.
option_d: Increases only if there is no wind.
explanation: Specific range (nautical miles per kilogram of fuel) for a jet aircraft increases with altitude because jet engines operate more efficiently at higher altitudes and low temperatures, and the drag is reduced.

question_text: (For this question use annex 032-1014A)Assuming constant L/D ratio, which of the diagrams provided correctly shows the movement of the ""Thrust Required Curve .(M1>M2).
option_a: c
option_c: b
option_d: d
explanation: Using the specific range versus weight and altitude diagram (Figure 1014A), curve (c) correctly represents the maximum range profile.

question_text: Long range cruise is a flight procedure which gives:
option_a: a specific range which is about 99% of maximum specific range and higher cruise speed.
option_b: a 1% higher TAS for maximum specific range.
option_c: an IAS which is 1% higher than the IAS for maximum specific range.
option_d: a specific range which is 99% of maximum specific range and a lower cruise speed.
explanation: Long Range Cruise (LRC) is a standard cruise procedure flown at a speed slightly faster than maximum range cruise (MRC). It yields a specific range of approximately 99% of MRC but provides a 3% to 5% increase in speed.

question_text: With zero wind, the angle of attack for maximum range for an aeroplane with turbojet engines is:
option_a: equal to that of maximum lift to drag ratio.
option_c: equal to that corresponding to zero induced drag.
option_d: lower than that of maximum lift to drag ratio.
explanation: For a jet aircraft, maximum range cruise (MRC) occurs at the speed where drag is minimized, which corresponds to the angle of attack for the maximum lift-to-drag ratio (L/D max).

question_text: Two identical turbojet aeroplane (whose specific fuel consumptions are considered to be equal) are at holding speed at the same altitude.The mass of the first aircraft is 130 000 kg and its hourly fuel consumption is 4300 kg/h. The mass of the second aircraft is 115 000 kg and its hourly fuel consumption is:
explanation: Using the cruise fuel flow charts for the two identical turbojets at the given weight and Mach number, the resulting fuel flow is 3804 kg/h.

question_text: A jet aeroplane is flying long range cruise. How does the specific range / fuel flow change?
option_a: Increase / decrease.
option_c: Decrease / increase.
option_d: Decrease / decrease.
explanation: As fuel is consumed and weight decreases, the specific range increases (more miles per kg) and the required fuel flow decreases.

question_text: During a cruise flight of a jet aeroplane at constant flight level and at the maximum range speed, the IAS / the drag will:
option_a: decrease / decrease.
option_c: increase / increase.
option_d: decrease / increase.
explanation: As weight decreases during a cruise at constant flight level, the required lift decreases, which reduces drag. Consequently, the required thrust decreases, and the fuel flow decreases.

question_text: The lowest point of the drag or thrust required curve of a jet aeroplane, respectively, is the point for
option_a: minimum drag.
option_c: maximum endurance.
option_d: minimum specific range.
explanation: The lowest point on the drag versus speed curve of a jet aircraft represents the speed for minimum drag (V_MD), which is also the speed for the maximum lift-to-drag ratio.

question_text: For a jet transport aeroplane, which of the following is the reason for the use of 'maximum range speed' ?
option_a: Minimum specific fuel consumption.
option_c: Longest flight duration.
option_d: Minimum drag.
explanation: Operating jet aircraft at high altitudes is highly efficient because the low ambient temperature increases the engine's thermodynamic efficiency, which minimizes the specific fuel consumption.

question_text: Consider the graphic representation of the power required versus true air speed (TAS), for a jet aeroplane with a given mass. When drawing the tangent out of the origin, the point of contact determines the speed of:
option_a: maximum endurance.
option_c: maximum specific range.
option_d: critical angle of attack.
explanation: On the power required versus TAS curve for a jet, the speed for maximum endurance (minimum fuel flow per hour) corresponds to the lowest point of the curve (minimum power required).

question_text: A jet aeroplane is performing a maximum range flight.The speed corresponds to:
option_a: the point of contact of the tangent from the origin to the Drag versus TAS curve.
option_c: the minimum required power. 169
option_d: the point of contact of the tangent from the origin to the power required (Pr) versus TAS curve.
explanation: For a jet aircraft, the speed for maximum range is found at the point of tangency of a line drawn from the origin to the thrust required (drag) curve.

question_text: In the drag versus TAS curve for a jet aeroplane, the speed for maximum range corresponds with:
option_a: the point of contact of the tangent from the origin to the drag curve.
option_b: the point of intersection of the parasite drag curve and the induced drag curve.
option_c: the point of contact of the tangent from the origin to the parasite drag curve.
option_d: the point of contact of the tangent from the origin to the induced drag curve.
explanation: In a drag versus speed curve, the speed for maximum range (which corresponds to the maximum ratio of speed to drag) is defined by the point of contact of a tangent line drawn from the origin to the curve.

question_text: The pilot of a jet aeroplane wants to use a minimum amount of fuel between two airfields. Which flight procedure should the pilot fly?
option_a: Maximum range.
option_c: Holding.
option_d: Long range.
explanation: To fly between two points using the absolute minimum amount of fuel, the pilot should fly at the Maximum Range cruise speed.

question_text: Which of the following is a reason to operate an aeroplane at 'long range speed'?
option_a: It is efficient to fly slightly faster than with maximum range speed.
option_b: In order to achieve speed stability.
option_c: The aircraft can be operated close to the buffet onset speed.
option_d: In order to prevent loss of speed stability and tuck-under.
explanation: Long range speed is slightly higher than the maximum range speed. It is preferred in airline operations because it offers a significant speed increase (typically 3-5% higher TAS) for a negligible penalty (only 1%) in specific range, thereby reducing block times and crew/operational costs.

question_text: ""Maximum endurance""
option_a: is achieved in unaccelerated level flight with minimum fuel consumption.
option_b: is the same as maximum specific range with wind correction.
option_c: can be flown in a steady climb only.
option_d: can be reached with the 'best rate of climb' speed in level flight.
explanation: Maximum endurance represents the maximum time an aircraft can remain airborne on a given amount of fuel. It is achieved in unaccelerated level flight at the speed where the fuel consumption rate (fuel flow per unit time) is minimized.

question_text: The speed for maximum endurance
option_a: is always lower than the speed for maximum specific range.
option_b: is the lower speed to achieve 99% of maximum specific range.
option_c: can either be higher or lower than the speed for maximum specific range.
option_d: is always higher than the speed for maximum specific range.
explanation: For jet aircraft, maximum endurance occurs at the speed for minimum thrust required (L/D max), whereas maximum range occurs at a higher speed (1.316 times the minimum drag speed). Therefore, the speed for maximum endurance is always lower than the speed for maximum range (maximum specific range).

question_text: Which of the equations below defines specific range (SR)?
option_a: SR = True Airspeed/Total Fuel Flow
option_c: SR = Mach Number/Total Fuel Flow
option_d: SR = Groundspeed/Total Fuel Flow
explanation: Specific range (SR) is defined as the distance traveled per unit of fuel consumed. It is calculated by dividing the True Airspeed (TAS) by the total hourly fuel flow (FF): SR = TAS / Fuel Flow.

question_text: Long range cruise is selected as
option_a: the higher speed to achieve 99% of maximum specific range in zero wind.
option_c: the climbing cruise with one or two engines inoperative.
option_d: specific range with tailwind.
explanation: Long range cruise (LRC) speed is defined as the speed above maximum range speed that achieves 99% of the maximum specific range. Operating at LRC provides a higher speed for a negligible 1% fuel mileage penalty in zero wind conditions.

question_text: The airspeed for jet aeroplanes at which power required is a minimum
option_a: is always lower than the minimum drag speed.
option_b: is always higher than the minimum drag speed.
option_c: is lower than the minimum drag speed in the climb and higher than the minimum drag speed in the descent.
option_d: is the same as the minimum drag speed.
explanation: For jet aeroplanes, the power required is the product of thrust required (drag) and true airspeed. The speed at which power required is a minimum (minimum power speed) is always lower than the speed at which drag is a minimum (minimum drag speed or L/D max speed).

question_text: Moving the center of gravity from the forward to the aft limit (gross mass, altitude and airspeed remain unchanged)
option_a: decreases the induced drag and reduces the power required.
option_c: affects neither drag nor power required.
option_d: increases the induced drag.
explanation: Moving the center of gravity (CG) aft decreases the downward aerodynamic tail load required for pitch equilibrium. This reduces the total lift the wings must produce, which decreases induced drag and reduces the engine power required to maintain level flight.

question_text: The centre of gravity near, but still within, the aft limit
option_a: improves the maximum range.
option_c: improves the longitudinal stabiity.
option_d: decreases the maximum range.
explanation: A center of gravity located near the aft limit decreases the downward force on the tail, reducing the required wing lift and its associated induced drag. This aerodynamic efficiency improves the aircraft's cruise fuel economy and maximum range.

question_text: The speed range between low speed buffet and high speed buffet
option_a: narrows with increasing mass and increasing altitude.
option_b: decreases with increasing mass and is independent of altitude.
option_c: is only limiting at low altitudes.
option_d: increases with increasing mass.
explanation: The speed range between low speed buffet (stalling boundary) and high speed buffet (compressibility boundary) represents the aircraft's safe speed margin at high altitudes. This margin narrows as mass increases (requiring higher lift coefficients/speeds) and as altitude increases (due to decreasing air density).

question_text: The danger associated with low speed and/or high speed buffet
option_a: limits the maneuvering load factor at high altitudes.
option_b: can be reduced by increasing the load factor.
option_c: exists only above MMO.
option_d: has to be considered at take-off and landing.
explanation: At high altitudes, the proximity of low speed buffet and high speed buffet limits the aircraft's maneuvering load factor. Any increase in load factor (due to turns or turbulence) increases the stalling speed, which can cause the aircraft to enter low speed buffet.

question_text: Which of the jet engine ratings below is not a certified rating?
option_a: Maximum Cruise Thrust
option_c: Go-Around Thrust
option_d: Maximum Take-off Thrust
explanation: Under certification rules, Maximum Take-off Thrust, Maximum Continuous Thrust, and Go-Around Thrust are certified engine ratings with strict operating time and temperature limits. Maximum Cruise Thrust is an operational rating set by the manufacturer for engine longevity, not a regulatory certified rating.

question_text: At constant thrust and constant altitude the fuel flow of a jet engine 170
option_a: increases slightly with increasing airspeed.
option_c: decreases slightly with increasing airspeed.
option_d: increases with decreasing OAT.
explanation: At constant thrust and constant altitude, the fuel flow of a jet engine increases slightly with increasing airspeed. This is primarily due to the ram recovery effect increasing the air mass flow through the engine, which requires more fuel to maintain the combustion ratio.

question_text: At a constant Mach number the thrust and the fuel flow of a jet engine
option_a: decrease in proportion to the ambient pressure at constant temperature.
option_c: are independent of outside air temperature (OAT).
option_d: increase in proportion to the ambient pressure at constant temperature.
explanation: At a constant Mach number, ambient air density changes in direct proportion to ambient pressure (if temperature is constant). As a result, both the thrust generated and the fuel flow of the jet engine decrease in proportion to the ambient pressure as altitude increases.

question_text: The thrust of a jet engine at constant RPM
option_a: increases in proportion to the airspeed.
option_b: does not change with changing altitude.
option_c: is independent of the airspeed.
option_d: is inversely proportional to the airspeed.
explanation: At a constant rotational speed (RPM) and constant altitude, jet engine thrust decreases as airspeed increases. This occurs because the inlet momentum drag increases and the relative acceleration of the exhaust gases through the nozzle decreases with higher forward speed.

question_text: The intersections of the thrust available and the drag curve are the operating points of the aeroplane
option_a: in unaccelerated level flight.
option_c: in accelerated level flight.
option_d: in unaccelerated climb.
explanation: In unaccelerated level flight, the thrust available must exactly equal the aerodynamic drag of the aircraft. Graphically, these operating points are located at the intersections of the thrust available curve and the total drag curve.
